title: Clinical Judgment Case Studies
description: Work through a patient case from arrival to outcome. Read the chart, answer, and watch the case unfold. Each case follows the six steps of clinical judgment.

cases.title: Shortness of breath after missed diuretics
cases.summary: Older adult with heart failure and rapid weight gain
cases.debrief: Key ideas: rapid weight gain plus crackles and JVD means fluid overload; airway and breathing come first; loop diuretics lower potassium, so check it before each dose; and successful diuresis can overshoot into orthostatic hypotension.

stages.title: Admission, 0800
stages.text: A 72-year-old client with heart failure (ejection fraction 30%) is admitted from the emergency department with shortness of breath. The client ran out of furosemide 5 days ago.

chart.title: Admission assessment
chart.text: Reports trouble breathing when lying flat and now sleeps in a recliner. Weight 84 kg (home weight 81 kg 4 days ago). Crackles bilaterally from bases to mid lungs. Jugular vein distention at 45 degrees. 3+ pitting edema of both lower legs. Alert and oriented x3. Speaks in short sentences.

Furosemide 40 mg IV push twice daily
Oxygen 2 to 4 L/min by nasal cannula, titrate to SpO2 at least 92%
Daily weight before breakfast, strict intake and output
Fluid restriction 1.5 L/day; 2 g sodium diet
Basic metabolic panel every morning
Potassium replacement per protocol

stages.title: Day 1, 1700
stages.text: The client has received one dose of IV furosemide and has put out 1,600 mL of urine.

chart.text: Weight 82.2 kg. Breathing easier; lying at 30 degrees. Crackles in bases only. Edema 1+. Client reports feeling dizzy when standing to use the bathroom.

cases.title: New confusion and fever in an older adult
cases.summary: Urinary source with low blood pressure and high lactate
cases.debrief: Key ideas: new confusion can be the first sign of sepsis in older adults; lactate above 2 mmol/L signals hypoperfusion; draw cultures but do not delay antibiotics; calculate weight-based fluid carefully; and reassess lungs during large-volume fluids.

stages.title: Arrival, 1400
stages.text: An 81-year-old client is brought in by family for new confusion that started this morning. Family reports the client has had burning on urination for 3 days.

chart.title: Triage
chart.text: Oriented to person only (baseline: fully oriented, lives alone). Skin warm and flushed. Urine in the bag is cloudy with a strong odor. Lungs clear. History: hypertension controlled with lisinopril.

rows: Positive leukocyte esterase and nitrites, many WBCs

chart.text:
Blood cultures x2 from two sites, urine culture
0.9% sodium chloride 30 mL/kg IV over 3 hours
Ceftriaxone 1 g IV now
Repeat lactate in 2 hours
Insert indwelling urinary catheter, hourly output
Fall precautions

stages.title: Reassessment, 1800
stages.text: The fluid bolus is complete and the first antibiotic dose was given at 1445.

chart.text: Oriented x3, asking for family. Urine output 45 mL/hr for the past 2 hours. New fine crackles in both lung bases.

cases.title: Vomiting and rapid breathing in a young adult with type 1 diabetes
cases.debrief: Key ideas: fluids first; know the potassium before insulin starts; insulin lowers serum potassium; add dextrose when glucose falls but keep the infusion running until the gap closes; and overlap basal insulin before stopping the drip.

stages.title: Arrival, 2200
stages.text: A 19-year-old client with type 1 diabetes arrives with 1 day of nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain. The client says they ran out of insulin and skipped doses for 2 days.

chart.title: Triage
chart.text: Drowsy but answers questions. Deep, rapid respirations. Fruity odor on breath. Dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor. Diffuse abdominal tenderness.

stages.title: Planning care
stages.text: The provider is entering the DKA order set.

stages.title: Insulin infusion, 2330
stages.text: One liter of 0.9% sodium chloride has infused. Repeat potassium is 5.0 mEq/L.

chart.text:
Regular insulin 0.1 units/kg/hr IV infusion (100 units in 100 mL 0.9% sodium chloride)
0.9% sodium chloride at 250 mL/hr
Glucose every hour; basic metabolic panel every 2 hours
Potassium replacement per DKA protocol
When glucose falls below 250 mg/dL, change fluids to dextrose 5% with 0.45% sodium chloride
More alert, nausea improving. Asking for water.

cases.title: Sudden weakness and trouble speaking
cases.summary: Older adult with atrial fibrillation and new one-sided weakness
cases.debrief: Key ideas: stroke care is a race against the clock, so note the last known well time; right-sided weakness with aphasia points to the left hemisphere; get a CT before anything that thins the blood; blood pressure must be under 185/110 before a thrombolytic, but not dropped too far; a sudden severe headache during the infusion means stop it; and keep the client NPO until a swallow screen is passed.

stages.title: Arrival, 0820
stages.text: A 68-year-old client is brought in by ambulance. A family member says the client was fine at breakfast at 0715, then dropped a coffee cup and could not get words out.

chart.title: Triage assessment
chart.text: Right side of the face droops when smiling. Right arm drifts down within 5 seconds; right leg weak. Understands questions and follows commands but struggles to find words and speech is slurred. History of atrial fibrillation; stopped apixaban 3 weeks ago because of cost. Last known well 0715.

chart.title: CT head without contrast
chart.text: No bleeding seen. Provider suspects acute ischemic stroke and plans IV alteplase. Weight 176 lb (80 kg).

Labetalol 10 mg IV now, may repeat once, to keep BP below 185/110 before alteplase
Alteplase 0.9 mg/kg IV (maximum 90 mg): 10% as IV bolus over 1 minute, the rest over 60 minutes
NPO until bedside swallow screen passed
Neuro checks and vital signs per stroke protocol
Admit to stroke unit

stages.title: Starting alteplase, 0905
stages.text: After one dose of labetalol, the blood pressure is 172/98 mm Hg. The nurse prepares the alteplase.

chart.text: Right arm now lifts against gravity and holds for 10 seconds. Speech clearer; still pauses for some words. Follow-up CT shows no bleeding. Bedside swallow screen: coughs and voice sounds wet after sips of water.

cases.title: Worsening breathlessness in a client with COPD
cases.summary: Older adult with a COPD flare, high carbon dioxide and a chest infection
cases.debrief: Key ideas: in a COPD flare, look for work of breathing and low oxygen first; read the ABG step by step; aim oxygen at 88 to 92% rather than 100%; sedatives and too much oxygen can both worsen carbon dioxide retention; new drowsiness means rising carbon dioxide and calls for urgent help; and expect high glucose from steroids and a fast heart rate from bronchodilators.

stages.title: Admission, 1100
stages.text: A 66-year-old client with COPD is admitted with 3 days of worsening shortness of breath and a cough that now brings up thick yellow-green sputum.

chart.title: Admission assessment
chart.text: Sitting forward with hands on knees, using neck and shoulder muscles to breathe. Pursed-lip breathing. Speaks 3 to 4 words at a time. Wheezes throughout with diminished sounds in the bases. Barrel-shaped chest and clubbed fingers. Alert and oriented x3. Quit smoking 2 years ago. Not on home oxygen.

Oxygen by Venturi mask, titrate to SpO2 88 to 92%
Albuterol and ipratropium by nebulizer every 4 hours and as needed
Methylprednisolone 40 mg IV every 12 hours
Sputum culture; then start prescribed IV antibiotic
Repeat ABG in 2 hours
Point-of-care glucose before meals and at bedtime

stages.title: Change in condition, 1400
stages.text: The nurse finds the client hard to wake. A family member turned the oxygen up "to help them rest."

chart.text: Opens eyes to loud voice, then drifts back to sleep. Oxygen found at 50% by Venturi mask.

stages.title: Day 3, 0900
stages.text: Two days have passed since the change in condition. The client is now on a nasal cannula.

chart.text: Awake and talking in full sentences. Fewer wheezes. Sputum thinner and lighter in color. Hands tremble after nebulizer treatments.

cases.title: Heavy bleeding after birth
cases.summary: Postpartum client with a soft uterus and rising blood loss
cases.debrief: Key ideas: a soft uterus above the umbilicus with heavy bleeding means uterine atony until proven otherwise; massage the fundus first while calling for help; weigh pads to measure blood loss (1 g is about 1 mL); check the history before uterotonic drugs (no carboprost with asthma, no methylergonovine with high blood pressure); and a fall in hemoglobin after the bleeding stops still needs follow-up.

stages.title: One hour after birth, 1500
stages.text: A 32-year-old client gave birth vaginally to her third baby 1 hour ago after a 14-hour labor induced with oxytocin. The newborn weighed 4.3 kg (9 lb 8 oz). Estimated blood loss at birth was 350 mL. History of mild asthma; uses an albuterol inhaler as needed.

chart.title: Postpartum assessment
chart.text: Fundus soft and boggy, 2 cm above the umbilicus, midline. Perineal pad soaked through in 15 minutes with several large clots. Skin cool and clammy. Says she feels "shaky and a little lightheaded." Reports cramping when the newborn breastfeeds. Lochia red.

stages.title: Measuring blood loss, 1515
stages.text: The nurse weighs everything soaked since the birth to find the quantitative blood loss.

chart.title: Weighed items
chart.text: Three soaked pads: 182 g, 176 g and 168 g (dry weight 22 g each). One soaked underpad: 340 g (dry weight 40 g).

Oxytocin infusion per postpartum hemorrhage protocol
Methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM now
Carboprost 250 mcg IM if bleeding continues
Second large-bore IV; type and crossmatch 2 units
CBC now and in 4 hours
Straight catheter to empty bladder
Fundus firm at the umbilicus, midline. One pad partly soaked in the past hour, no large clots. Urine output 40 mL/hr. Feels lightheaded when sitting up at the side of the bed.

cases.title: Vomiting and diarrhea in a toddler
cases.summary: Toddler with gastroenteritis and signs of severe dehydration
cases.debrief: Key ideas: weight loss is the best measure of dehydration in children; a fast heart rate and slow capillary refill appear before blood pressure falls; give an isotonic bolus of 20 mL/kg and reassess; check glucose in a lethargic child; do not add potassium until the child is passing urine; use oral rehydration solution, not juice; and avoid antidiarrheal drugs in young children.

stages.title: Arrival, 1000
stages.text: An 18-month-old is brought in by a parent after 2 days of vomiting and watery diarrhea. Several children at the child's daycare have been sick.

chart.title: Triage assessment
chart.text: Lethargic but wakes when touched; weak cry with no tears. Lips and mouth dry. Eyes look sunken. Capillary refill 3 seconds. Last wet diaper about 10 hours ago. Weight 10.8 kg today; weighed 12.0 kg at a clinic visit 1 week ago. Clings to parent.

0.9% sodium chloride 20 mL/kg IV bolus over 20 minutes; reassess and repeat once if needed
Dextrose 10% 5 mL/kg IV for glucose below 60 mg/dL
Then D5 0.9% sodium chloride at maintenance rate; add potassium chloride 20 mEq/L once voiding
Ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg IV once
Weigh all diapers; strict intake and output
Oral rehydration solution in small amounts once vomiting settles

stages.title: Fluid calculations, 1035
stages.text: The nurse uses today's weight of 10.8 kg for all calculations.

stages.title: Six hours later, 1630
stages.text: The child is now on maintenance IV fluid.

chart.text: Awake, playing with a toy and crying with tears. Mouth moist. Capillary refill under 2 seconds. Keeping down small sips of oral rehydration solution. Two loose stools in the past 4 hours.

questions.stem: Which findings require immediate follow-up by the nurse? Select all that apply.

options.text: Crackles from the bases to the mid lungs
Alert and oriented to person, place and time
Weight gain of 3 kg in 4 days

questions.explanation: Low oxygen saturation, crackles that reach the mid lungs, tachypnea and rapid weight gain all point to fluid backing up into the lungs. They need follow-up now. A 3 kg gain is about 3 L of retained fluid.

why.F: Within normal range, though it should be watched once diuresis starts.

questions.explanation: Breathing comes first. Fluid in the alveoli is lowering oxygenation (SpO2 89%, RR 26) and can progress to respiratory failure. The other problems are real but less immediately life-threatening.

questions.stem: For each potential intervention, indicate whether it is indicated, contraindicated or non-essential for the client at this time.

rows.text: Place the client in high Fowler position
Give furosemide IV as ordered
Infuse 0.9% sodium chloride 1,000 mL bolus
Monitor strict intake and output and daily weight
Encourage 3 L of oral fluid per day
Teach the full low-sodium meal plan now

questions.explanation: The goal is to remove fluid and ease breathing: upright position, IV loop diuretic, and close tracking of output and weight. Extra fluid would worsen overload. Diet teaching matters, but it is not essential while the client is short of breath and can be done once they are stable.

why.r3: A fluid bolus adds volume to a client who is already overloaded.
why.r5: Heart failure orders here include a 1.5 L/day fluid restriction.
why.r6: Teaching works best once the client can breathe comfortably and focus.

questions.stem: The evening furosemide dose is due. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Hold the furosemide and give the client extra oral fluids
Give the furosemide as scheduled and recheck potassium in the morning
Report the potassium of 3.2 mEq/L and follow the replacement protocol before giving the furosemide

questions.explanation: Loop diuretics waste potassium. A level of 3.2 mEq/L is low and raises the risk of dysrhythmias, so the nurse reports it and replaces potassium per protocol or order before more diuretic is given. The client still needs diuresis, so the dose is not simply dropped.

why.A: Extra fluid works against the fluid restriction and the diuresis goal.
why.B: Giving more diuretic without addressing low potassium can drop it further.
why.C: Nurses do not change the dose without an order.

questions.order: 0.9% sodium chloride 30 mL/kg IV over 3 hours

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing the first dose of ceftriaxone. Which action is most important before giving it?

options.text: Give acetaminophen first to lower the fever
Make sure blood cultures have been drawn, without delaying the antibiotic
Wait for the urine culture result to choose the right antibiotic

questions.explanation: Cultures drawn before the first antibiotic dose give the best chance of identifying the organism. In sepsis the antibiotic should not be held for long waiting on cultures, so they are drawn quickly and the drug is started right away.

why.A: Antipyretics can be given, but they are not a prerequisite and do not treat the infection.
why.B: The fever is already documented and does not change the action.
why.D: Culture results take a day or more; waiting would dangerously delay treatment.

questions.stem: After the fluid bolus and first antibiotic dose, indicate whether each finding shows the client is improving or needs follow-up.

rows.text: Blood pressure 108/64 mm Hg
Repeat lactate 1.9 mmol/L
Urine output 45 mL/hr
Oriented to person, place and time
New crackles in both lung bases with SpO2 90%

questions.stem: Complete the statement by choosing from the lists.
questions.template: The client has {{1}}. The serum potassium is high because {{2}}, so once insulin is started, the potassium is expected to {{3}}.

options.text: the kidneys are retaining potassium normally
acidosis and lack of insulin shift potassium out of cells
the client eats a high-potassium diet

questions.explanation: High glucose, ketones, low pH and low bicarbonate with an anion gap are DKA. Potassium leaves the cells in acidosis and without insulin, so the serum level looks high even though total body potassium is usually low. Insulin drives potassium back into cells, so the level falls.

questions.stem: For each potential order, indicate whether the nurse should anticipate it or not anticipate it for this client.

rows.text: 0.9% sodium chloride IV bolus
Confirm potassium is at least 3.3 mEq/L before starting the insulin infusion
Check blood glucose every hour
Sodium bicarbonate IV for a pH of 7.18
Add dextrose to the IV fluids once glucose falls to about 250 mg/dL
Regular insulin by IV push every 15 minutes until glucose is normal

questions.explanation: DKA care centers on isotonic fluids, a continuous low-dose IV insulin infusion started only once potassium is safe, hourly glucose checks, and dextrose once glucose falls so insulin can keep clearing ketones without causing hypoglycemia. Bicarbonate is reserved for very severe acidosis, and repeated IV insulin pushes risk rapid drops in glucose and potassium.

why.r4: Bicarbonate is generally reserved for pH below about 7.0.
why.r6: A steady infusion is used; the goal is a gradual glucose decline.

questions.explanation: Sudden weakness on one side with speech trouble in a client with atrial fibrillation who stopped an anticoagulant fits an acute stroke, likely from a clot. Each side of the brain controls the opposite side of the body, and language centers are usually on the left, so right-sided weakness plus aphasia points to the left hemisphere.

questions.stem: Which action is the priority for this client right now?

options.text: Give aspirin by mouth to prevent clot growth
Offer sips of water to check the swallow
Lower the blood pressure to below 120/80 mm Hg
Get the client to a noncontrast CT of the head as quickly as possible

questions.explanation: Treatment depends on knowing whether the stroke is from a clot or a bleed, and only imaging can show that. Every minute counts, so the CT comes first.

why.A: Aspirin before a CT could worsen a bleeding stroke, and the swallow has not been screened.
why.B: The client must stay NPO until a formal swallow screen; slurred speech raises aspiration risk.
why.C: Dropping the pressure too far can reduce blood flow to brain tissue that can still be saved.

questions.stem: For each potential intervention, indicate whether it is indicated, contraindicated or non-essential for the client at this time.

rows.text: Keep the client NPO until the swallow screen is passed
Give labetalol IV as prescribed and recheck the blood pressure
Give aspirin 325 mg by mouth now
Lower the blood pressure quickly to 120/80 mm Hg
Do neuro checks and vital signs per stroke protocol
Teach about a heart-healthy diet for atrial fibrillation

questions.explanation: Before alteplase, the blood pressure must be below 185/110 mm Hg, the client stays NPO, and neuro status is checked often so any change is caught early. Antiplatelet drugs are held, and teaching can wait until the client is stable.

why.r3: Antiplatelet drugs are not given around thrombolytic therapy (usually not for 24 hours after) because of bleeding risk, and the swallow is unscreened.
why.r4: Only enough lowering to get under the treatment limit is wanted; a large drop can extend the stroke.
why.r6: Useful later, but it does not change care in the next hour.

questions.stem: The client weighs 80 kg. The order is alteplase 0.9 mg/kg IV (maximum 90 mg), with 10% of the total dose given as an IV bolus over 1 minute. How many mg will the nurse give as the bolus?
questions.order: Alteplase 0.9 mg/kg IV (maximum 90 mg): 10% as IV bolus over 1 minute, the rest over 60 minutes
questions.formula: Total dose = kg x mg/kg (check the maximum); Bolus = total x 0.10

steps.explain: Total dose. 72 mg is under the 90 mg maximum, so the full amount is used.
The bolus is 10% of the total.

questions.explanation: Total dose 80 x 0.9 = 72 mg. The bolus is 10%, so 7.2 mg over 1 minute, and the remaining 64.8 mg infuses over 60 minutes. Double-check weight-based thrombolytic doses with a second nurse per policy.
mistakes: Giving 10% of the 90 mg maximum (9 mg) instead of 10% of the calculated dose.
Using the weight in pounds (176 x 0.9 = 158.4 mg), which is far above the maximum.

questions.stem: Twenty minutes into the alteplase infusion, which finding requires the nurse to stop the infusion right away?

options.text: Sudden severe headache with new vomiting
A small amount of oozing at the IV site
The client asks for a drink of water

questions.explanation: A sudden severe headache, vomiting, a jump in blood pressure or a drop in level of consciousness during a thrombolytic can mean bleeding in the brain. Stop the infusion, notify the provider immediately and expect an emergency CT.

why.B: Minor oozing is expected; apply gentle pressure and keep watching.
why.C: Below 180/105 mm Hg is the usual goal during and after alteplase; keep monitoring.
why.D: The client stays NPO until a swallow screen is passed, but this is not a reason to stop the drug.

questions.stem: Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Apply a non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min to reach an SpO2 of 100%
Encourage the client to drink more fluids to thin the sputum
Give oxygen titrated to an SpO2 of 88 to 92% and help the client sit upright
Hold oxygen to avoid suppressing the drive to breathe

questions.explanation: Hypoxemia is the immediate threat, so oxygen is needed now. In a client who retains carbon dioxide, a target of 88 to 92% corrects dangerous hypoxemia while lowering the risk of making the carbon dioxide level climb. Sitting upright helps the diaphragm work.

why.A: High-flow oxygen aimed at 100% can raise carbon dioxide further in COPD.
why.B: Hydration helps later but does not treat the low oxygen now.
why.D: Never withhold oxygen from a hypoxemic client; titrate it instead.

questions.explanation: New drowsiness, a slower breathing rate and a pH of 7.24 with PaCO2 72 mm Hg mean carbon dioxide is building up and the client is tiring. Too much oxygen likely contributed. why.C: A nebulizer does not fix a failing breathing effort.

options.text: a 4.3 kg newborn after a long oxytocin-induced labor

questions.explanation: Atony, a uterus that does not stay contracted, is the most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage, and a soft fundus above the umbilicus is its key sign. A large baby stretches the uterus, and a long labor with oxytocin can tire the muscle, both raising the risk. Being a third birth adds to it.

why.1: A laceration usually causes steady bright red bleeding with a firm uterus. There is no sign of a clotting problem, and platelets are normal.
why.2: Asthma does not cause bleeding, but it matters for drug choice.

options.text: Weigh the pads to measure the blood loss
Insert a straight catheter to empty the bladder
Leave the room to phone the provider
Massage the fundus firmly while supporting the lower uterus, and call for help

questions.explanation: Fundal massage makes the uterus contract and is the fastest way to slow bleeding from atony. Supporting the lower uterus with the other hand keeps it from being pushed down. Use the call light or ask a coworker so the nurse never leaves the client.

why.A: Measuring loss is important, but treating the bleeding comes first.
why.B: A full bladder can keep the uterus from contracting, but massage comes first.
why.C: The nurse should stay with a bleeding client and call for help from the bedside.

why.r6: Important before discharge, not during an emergency.

questions.explanation: Weight loss is the best guide: 1.2 kg lost from 12.0 kg is 10%. A loss of 10% or more with lethargy, slow capillary refill and very little urine is severe dehydration.

rows.text: Give the 0.9% sodium chloride bolus as prescribed
Treat the glucose of 58 mg/dL with the prescribed dextrose
Start maintenance fluid with potassium chloride right away
Offer apple juice to replace fluid
Give an over-the-counter antidiarrheal medicine
Weigh every diaper

questions.explanation: An isotonic bolus restores circulating volume, low glucose in a lethargic child must be treated, and weighing diapers measures output (1 g is about 1 mL). Potassium waits until the kidneys are working.

why.r3: Potassium is added only after the child voids. If the kidneys are not making urine, potassium can build up to a dangerous level.
why.r4: Juice is high in sugar and low in sodium and can make diarrhea worse. Use oral rehydration solution.
why.r5: Antidiarrheal drugs are not recommended for young children with infectious diarrhea and can cause harm.
